why: Server i needs t_i = ceil(health[i] / k) virus-seconds and costs request[i] requests for every second it is still up, so the total is the sum of request[i] times the second it dies: weighted completion-time scheduling. The exchange argument (Smith's rule) says kill servers in increasing t_i / request[i].
hints: Every second you pay the sum of the requests of the servers still alive. So a server's cost is request[i] times the second it goes down.
Put all viruses on one server until it dies (splitting only delays everyone). Swap two adjacent servers in the kill order and compare: A should go before B when t_A * req_B < t_B * req_A.
Compute t_i = ceil(health[i]/k), sort by that ratio using cross-multiplication (no floats), accumulate elapsed time and add request[i] * elapsed. Add 1 for the final request. O(n log n).
pitfalls: Do not forget the one extra request after all servers are down.
Compare ratios with cross-multiplication; floating division can mis-order ties.
Kill time is a ceiling: health 4 with k = 3 takes 2 seconds.
statement:
There are n servers. Server i serves request[i] requests per second and has health health[i].

Every second the developers send as many requests as all servers that are still up can serve (the sum of request[i] over the live servers). Along with them they send one virus to a server of their choice, reducing its health by k. A server is down once its health is ≤ 0.

After all servers are down, one more request is sent to conclude the failure. Return the minimum total number of requests sent.

Worked example: request = [3, 4], health = [4, 6], k = 3. Server 0 needs ceil(4/3) = 2 viruses, server 1 needs ceil(6/3) = 2.

  1. Seconds 1 and 2: both servers up, 3 + 4 = 7 requests each; viruses hit server 1, which goes down. Total 14.
  2. Seconds 3 and 4: only server 0 up, 3 requests each; viruses hit server 0, which goes down. Total 14 + 6 = 20.
  3. One final request: 21. (Killing server 0 first would give 7+7+4+4+1 = 23.)
constraints:
• n == request.length == health.length
  • 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5 (not stated in the source)
  • 1 ≤ request[i], health[i], k ≤ 10^9 (not stated in the source)
